title: Utility-scale electromagnetic delivery of power without a conductor

concept.text: The innovation would deliver utility-scale electricity across a distance using a directed electromagnetic beam. A transmitter would turn electrical input into microwave or laser energy, direct it toward a receiver, and recover electrical output at the destination. The target is sustained, useful power delivery with acceptable losses, availability and safety, rather than simply detecting a transmitted signal.

Scope synthesis: the central capability is power transmission across a gap where a line or cable is a meaningful alternative, or where a connecting conductor cannot practically be installed. Microwave and optical systems are different implementations of that capability. Electricity generation at either end, orbital infrastructure and grid integration are additional system functions; a successful beam would not by itself supply them.

significance.text: If sustained utility-scale beaming became practical, its direct significance would be logistical: electricity could reach suitable remote receivers, isolated sites or moving platforms without a connecting conductor. This could expand the options for supplying locations cut off by terrain, damaged infrastructure or operational constraints. The supplied project accounts motivate such applications, but do not demonstrate their utility-scale deployment.

Impact synthesis: the revolutionary possibility is an additional way to route substantial electrical power, not an automatic replacement for transmission networks. Ordinary corridors could continue to favor conductors wherever they offer better cost, efficiency, availability and safety. The value of a beam would depend on the application, including the infrastructure it avoids and the operating restrictions it introduces.

Space-based solar power is a conditional downstream application. Delivering collected orbital energy to Earth would require power beaming alongside launch, large-scale manufacturing, assembly, orbital transfer, durable hardware and system operation. A successful terrestrial link would not establish continuous orbital solar electricity through terrestrial night and weather, nor demonstrate that the complete orbital system is economical.

NASA's 2024 first-order assessment examined two representative space-solar-power designs normalized to 2 GW. It found baseline lifecycle electricity costs potentially about 12 to 80 times those of terrestrial renewable alternatives. More favorable scenarios combined improvements in launch, manufacturing, solar-cell efficiency, hardware lifetime and orbital transfer. These are results for the studied designs and assumptions, not a universal cost bound or proof that every possible design must achieve exactly those improvements. The supplied review supports this interpretation through the NTRS abstract and a shortened presentation, rather than the underlying complete technical study.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target breakthrough is the integration of sustained delivered power, useful total efficiency, reliable operation and an accepted safety case at utility scale. Existing demonstrations establish important parts of the transmission chain, but the supplied evidence does not establish that this complete capability has been achieved. It also does not establish its absence across all projects as of November 1, 2026.

Engineering synthesis from the research: a practical link must reconcile beam spreading and transmitter and receiver aperture size with pointing accuracy, receiver motion, atmospheric propagation and weather. It must also control spillover and unintended exposure. Diffraction is relevant to beam spreading, but the supplied review does not substantiate a complete quantitative aperture analysis, exposure assessment or microwave-versus-laser comparison. These remain design questions to resolve for a specified wavelength, distance, site and power level.

Atmospheric effects are an explicitly identified challenge in DARPA's optical development account. More broadly, an assessment of useful efficiency must follow energy through beam generation, propagation and conversion back to electricity. DARPA's reported optical-to-electrical efficiency covers only part of that chain, illustrating why a strong receiver result or propagation result alone cannot establish electricity-input-to-electricity-output performance.

System synthesis: scaling power also requires managing conversion losses and associated heat, maintaining beam control during interruptions or receiver movement, and demonstrating safe behavior when the intended path is obstructed or control is lost. For orbital applications, these transmission requirements sit alongside the aerospace and production challenges identified by NASA. The supplied material does not provide a complete validated engineering solution or safety analysis for these combined requirements.

current_state.text: The research attributes an X-band microwave demonstration reported in 2022 to the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory: 1.6 kW of electrical output at 1,046 m, with 73 percent radiofrequency-to-direct-current conversion at the rectenna. It also attributes to the same paper a historical comparison describing W. C. Brown's 2.39 GHz result of 34 kW received at 1.55 km as the highest earlier microwave power. These numerical claims are preserved as attributed results, but the cited paper was not captured in the supplied source record, so the review could not verify its contents, measurement boundaries or historical ranking. Even if confirmed, rectenna conversion efficiency would not establish total electricity-to-electricity efficiency.

On May 16, 2025, DARPA reported that its POWER program delivered more than 800 W during a 30-second laser transmission over 8.6 km. The same account reported efficiency above 20 percent from laser optical output to receiver electrical output at shorter distances. It did not assign that efficiency to the 8.6 km result. The demonstrated power, duration and distance therefore should be kept separate from the shorter-distance efficiency measurement, and neither measurement establishes total electrical-input-to-electrical-output efficiency.

Caltech's June 1, 2023 account reported that MAPLE powered LEDs at receivers about a foot from its transmitter in orbit. It also reported detection of a transmitted signal on a Pasadena rooftop on May 22, at the expected time and frequency and with the predicted frequency shift. These are distinct achievements: local power transfer within the orbital experiment and detection of a signal transmitted from orbit to Earth. The rooftop detection does not establish useful utility-scale electrical delivery.

NASA's 2024 material characterized space-to-ground power beaming as nascent and analyzed prospective large systems. Its modeled 2 GW designs are study scenarios, not demonstrations of operating power delivery. The available evidence described in the review consists of the substantive NTRS abstract and a complete shortened 16-page presentation; it does not include the underlying full technical study.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record establishes the dated DARPA and Caltech reports, while leaving the microwave figures unverified here. It supplies no bounded search record showing whether a later continuous megawatt demonstration existed by November 1, 2026. Consequently, it supports neither a claim that the complete capability has been achieved nor a cutoff-wide assertion that no such achievement exists. Missing evidence for the NRL paper is not evidence that its reported results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed milestone: demonstrate a continuous link delivering at least about one megawatt of electrical output over a distance where a line or cable is a meaningful alternative. Publish electricity-input-to-electricity-output efficiency and measure availability over weeks. This is an author-selected milestone for evaluating utility-scale progress, not an official threshold or an established industry standard.
completion_criteria.label: Continuous electrical delivery of at least about one megawatt

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement requirements: report input and delivered power, auxiliary electrical loads, losses at each conversion stage, operating conditions, interruptions and measurement uncertainty. Distinguish efficiency while transmitting from energy delivered across the full observation period, so shutdowns and weather-related interruptions remain visible. Choose and justify a quantitative efficiency acceptance threshold before the test; the supplied material does not establish one.
completion_criteria.label: Full electrical performance accounting against a predeclared efficiency acceptance threshold

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and reproducibility requirements: obtain acceptance of the safety case from the relevant regulator, document beam containment and exposure controls, and demonstrate responses to obstruction, pointing errors and loss of control. Independent verification and repeat operation under declared conditions would make the result more convincing. Tests should state the distances, weather conditions, receiver configurations and operating restrictions actually covered. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth within that envelope, rather than universal safety or availability.
completion_criteria.label: Regulator-accepted safety case with demonstrated controls and declared operating limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed later milestone: evaluate sustained delivery at hundreds of megawatts to gigawatts before claiming consequences for bulk transmission networks. This would require application-specific comparisons of infrastructure cost, losses, availability, land or aperture requirements and safety restrictions. An orbital signal detection or a brief transmission delivering more than 800 W would not meet the proposed megawatt milestone. The earlier gigawatt, tens-to-hundreds-of-kilometers and above-80-percent figures can only be treated as possible performance ambitions; their historical provenance and authority are not established in the supplied record.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained delivery at hundreds of megawatts to gigawatts evaluated

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — PWR-01, Practical dissipationless conductors and windings for bulk power systems: both concepts concern delivering or handling substantial electrical power with acceptable losses. PWR-01 retains conducting paths and windings; PWR-03 transmits energy across a gap as electromagnetic radiation. Better conductors could improve equipment associated with a beam system or strengthen the competing wired option, but would not resolve beam propagation, capture or exposure requirements.

Roster-based synthesis — PWR-02, Solid-state conversion of heat to utility electricity: this concerns converting thermal energy into electrical output, while PWR-03 concerns transporting energy between locations. A thermal converter could supply a transmitter, but its generation performance would remain distinct from beam-link efficiency. Neither capability establishes the other.

Roster-based synthesis — PWR-04, Site-independent storage from multi-day weather through seasonal imbalance: storage shifts energy across time, while PWR-03 would move it across space. Storage could buffer a receiver during beam interruptions or variations in generation. A successful beam link would not itself solve multi-day or seasonal energy imbalance, and storage would not establish long-distance beam delivery.

Roster-based synthesis — PWR-05, An interconnection that no longer depends on synchronous machines: this concerns coordinated grid operation, whereas PWR-03 concerns a transmission mechanism. A utility-scale receiver would still need an electrical interface appropriate to the receiving network. Demonstrating a beam would not establish the stability, protection or control of a wider interconnection.

Space-based solar power overlaps with PWR-03 because it requires energy transfer from an orbital collection system to a receiver. It is nevertheless a broader system concept, incorporating generation, launch, assembly, lifetime and orbital operations. NASA's representative designs illustrate this added scope. Terrestrial power beaming and orbital solar power should therefore remain distinct, even where they share transmission technology.

change_log.change: Preserved PWR-03's identity and expanded the explanation around sustained utility-scale electrical delivery.
change_log.reason: The concept remains meaningful even where individual supporting assertions require qualification.

change_log.change: Removed the exhaustive 'third carrier' taxonomy and made logistical and network impacts conditional.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports an additional delivery mechanism, not an exhaustive classification or inevitable replacement of conductors.

change_log.change: Retained the NRL and Brown quantitative claims with explicit attribution and verification limits.
change_log.reason: The research supplied useful numerical detail, but the cited microwave paper had no captured evidence available to the review. Omitting the figures would lose information; presenting them as verified would overstate support.

change_log.change: Separated DARPA's 8.6 km power-and-duration result from its shorter-distance efficiency result and clarified the optical-to-electrical boundary.
change_log.reason: The supplied account does not establish greater-than-20-percent efficiency at the record distance or total electricity-to-electricity efficiency.

change_log.change: Distinguished MAPLE's local orbital power transfer from its Earth-bound signal detection.
change_log.reason: Lighting nearby LEDs and detecting a rooftop signal demonstrate different capabilities; neither establishes utility electricity delivery from orbit.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims about the absence of grid-duty demonstrations through the cutoff with a bounded evidence statement.
change_log.reason: No freshness search record was supplied, so the dated results cannot establish the global state of the field on November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Qualified NASA's cost range, favorable scenarios and source access.
change_log.reason: The 12-to-80-times comparison concerns two representative 2 GW designs. Combined modeled improvements are not universal necessary conditions, and the supplied review used an abstract and shortened presentation.

change_log.change: Preserved diffraction, aperture, pointing, weather, spillover and exposure considerations as engineering synthesis with explicit limits.
change_log.reason: These are useful research distinctions, but the review did not substantiate a complete quantitative trade-off or safety analysis.

change_log.change: Clarified delivered electrical power, full efficiency accounting, reproducibility and operating boundaries in the proposed completion criteria.
change_log.reason: The proposed milestone needs measurable boundaries without implying that its numerical thresholds are official or that finite tests establish universal performance.

change_log.change: Avoided adopting the review's 'sub-kilowatt' description of DARPA's result.
change_log.reason: The supplied report states more than 800 W without providing an upper bound; that wording alone does not establish output below one kilowatt.

change_log.change: Added distinct relationships to all four other supplied roster entries and separated orbital solar power from the transmission capability.
change_log.reason: Generation, transmission, storage, conductor performance and grid operation overlap at system interfaces but remain different innovations.

unresolved_issues: The NRL paper's 1.6 kW output, 1,046 m distance, 73 percent rectenna efficiency, experimental duration and measurement boundaries remain unverified in the supplied evidence.
The Brown 34 kW, 1.55 km and 2.39 GHz figures, including the scope of the historical ranking, require verification from the uncaptured microwave source.
No bounded freshness search establishes whether sustained utility-scale power beaming had been demonstrated elsewhere by November 1, 2026.
The supplied DARPA account does not establish efficiency at 8.6 km, total electricity-to-electricity efficiency, or sustained availability beyond the reported 30-second transmission.
A quantitative efficiency acceptance threshold, test distance and detailed availability requirement remain to be selected for the proposed megawatt milestone.
The provenance of the earlier gigawatt, tens-to-hundreds-of-kilometers and above-80-percent performance targets is unresolved; they are not treated as official completion criteria.
The supplied evidence does not resolve the full wavelength-specific aperture, weather, exposure and regulatory trade-offs for a utility-scale implementation.
NASA's underlying complete technical study was not available in the supplied review, limiting assessment beyond its abstract and shortened presentation.
The optional Caltech PDF was an unrelated institutional poster and supplies no MAPLE evidence; the relevant HTML account remains the basis for the stated experimental results.
